tier_reason: Chapter06/09_function.C is public Google Benchmark code comparing the book's Function (16-byte inline buffer plus function-pointer executor) with std::function on the same callables, but the repo carries no results, compiler, flags or CPU; the ns figures exist only in the book (first-party), so C.

corrections.workload: Google Benchmark of invoking a callable with four int arguments: the book's Function class (16-byte inline buffer plus a function-pointer executor; accepts only trivially copyable, trivially destructible callables) against std::function<int(int,int,int,int)> holding the same callable, in three pairs: a noinline free function through an invoke helper (BM_invoke_fast_function / BM_invoke_std_function), a lambda capturing x by reference through the helper (BM_invoke_fast_lambda / BM_invoke_std_lambda) and the same lambda called directly (BM_fast_lambda / BM_std_lambda), with plain lambda, inlined function and virtual-call rows as reference; results kept alive with DoNotOptimize and ClobberMemory.
corrections.caveats: Narrower than std::function: Function static_asserts that the callable is trivially copyable, trivially destructible and at most 16 bytes, has no heap fallback, no target() and no empty check before the call (a null Function throws through its default executor). The benchmarked lambda captures by reference ([&], an 8-byte capture), which also fits std::function's small-buffer storage, so neither side allocates and the gap is call-path overhead only. First-party book numbers: the repo has no results, build line or CPU, and the file holds several pairs (BM_invoke_fast_function/BM_invoke_std_function, BM_invoke_fast_lambda/BM_invoke_std_lambda, BM_fast_lambda/BM_std_lambda, plus BM_lambda, BM_invoke_lambda, BM_invoke_virtual); which rows the book's 0.884 / 1.33 / 0.219 ns figures come from is not stated in the repo. Teaching example, not a packaged library. Tier C.

notes: Code matches the description; record said value-capturing lambda but the lambdas capture by reference ([&]), corrected in workload. Category smart-pointers-and-refcount fits poorly for a std::function replacement; orchestrator may want a category override (callables/utilities). Repo metadata confirmed on github.com: MIT, 137 stars, not fork/archived, last commit 2024-08-29 (stale).

tier_reason: Chapter06/07_smartptr.C (with 07_smartptr.h and 07_smartptr_ext.C) benchmarks smartptr_te_static and smartptr_te_vtable against std::shared_ptr with a custom deleter, std::make_shared, std::unique_ptr and a raw pointer, but the repo shows no results, compiler, flags or CPU; numbers are the book's own, so C.

corrections.caveats: Not feature-equal: std::shared_ptr allocates a control block and does atomic reference counting, while the book's pointers have unique ownership. The benchmark does contain closer like-for-like rows: BM_smartptr_te (the book's own type-erased deleter on the heap, virtual call) and the local-buffer virtual variants BM_smartptr_te_lb and BM_smartptr_te_lb0, plus std::unique_ptr<int, deleter> (no type erasure); a std::unique_ptr with a std::function deleter is not benchmarked. Net overhead over the raw-pointer floor is only about 0.9 to 1.7 ns (derived from the relayed numbers), so most of the gap to shared_ptr is the control-block allocation and atomic counting. Factory functions sit in a separate translation unit (07_smartptr_ext.C) so new/delete cannot be elided, which keeps the rows comparable. smartptr_te_static and smartptr_te_vtable declare no copy or move operations, so the implicit copy would double-delete: teaching code, not a drop-in smart pointer. The book's chapter 10 repeats the idea with different absolute numbers (21.0, 44.2 and 22.3 ns, recorded in the no-evidence file), so absolute figures vary between runs or machines. First-party, compiler and CPU not stated in the repo. Tier C.

notes: Benchmark code matches the record; corrected the caveat that the like-for-like baseline is absent (the book's heap type-erased smartptr_te row is in the file). Comparison against shared_ptr is apples-to-oranges (shared vs unique ownership); unique_ptr row is the fairer stdlib baseline and the book's pointers do not beat it. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 137 stars, last commit 2024-08-29 (stale).

tier_reason: Chapter11/11_scopeguard_te_benchmark.C benchmarks the template ScopeGuard against a std::function-based guard, a function-pointer local-buffer guard and explicit delete, but the repo has no results, compiler, flags or CPU; numbers come only from the book, so C.

corrections.workload: Google Benchmark of a scope guard that deletes a pointer: template ScopeGuard (callable stored by value, no type erasure) against a guard holding a std::function<void()>, a local-buffer function-pointer guard (ScopeGuardTypeErasedFast) and a hand-written explicit delete, in four cases: noop (guard on a null pointer created outside the loop), nodelete (rand() call, pointer stays null), nodelete2 (two pointers) and delete (rand() call plus new int and delete every iteration).
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the book's own std::function guard, not a library guard (Boost.ScopeExit, folly::ScopeGuard, std::experimental::scope_exit), which are template designs like the winner and were not benchmarked. Each nodelete and delete iteration calls rand(), so the about 4.5 ns explicit and template rows are mostly rand(). Possible harness asymmetry (inferred from the source and the relayed numbers, not measured here): in BM_delete_explicit and BM_delete_template the new int(42) and delete sit in the same inlined scope, so the compiler may elide the allocation pair, which would explain why those rows (4.54 and 4.56 ns) equal the nodelete rows (4.48 and 4.50 ns); the std::function guard calls the delete through type erasure, so its allocation cannot be elided. The 2.9x delete-case ratio may therefore overstate the guard overhead; the nodelete case (6.29 against 4.50 ns, about 1.8 ns of std::function overhead) is the cleaner comparison. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated, first-party. Tier C.

notes: Code matches the record; the old caveat assumed the explicit-delete row contains a real new/delete pair, but it equals the nodelete row within 0.06 ns, which points to allocation elision on the explicit and template sides only; enricher should check this with a build or compiler-explorer reasoning.
